question: What does the Bible say about the Lord's Supper?
intro: The Lord's Supper is the meal of bread and cup that Christ's followers keep in remembrance of him, as Jesus took bread and a cup at his last meal with his disciples, which Luke calls “this Passover” (Luke 22:15, 19-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). It is also called communion or Holy Communion, the Eucharist, the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42), and, in the churches that use those names for the service, the Mass (Catholic) and the Divine Liturgy (Eastern Orthodox). Every church set out here keeps it, and they read the text differently on what the bread and the cup are. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that Jesus took bread and a cup at his last meal with his disciples, called the bread his body and the cup his blood of the covenant, and told them to do this in remembrance of him (1 Corinthians 11:25); that those who eat the bread and drink the cup proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (11:26); that each person is to examine himself first (11:28); and that the many who share the one loaf are one body (10:17). The readings differ on what the bread and the cup are, and so on what the words “This is My body” and “a participation in the body of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:16) mean. They differ also on three related points that this page names and does not set out as readings: whether the Supper is a sacrifice, who may receive it, and how often it is kept.

passages.quote: do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.
passages.note: Paul passes on Jesus' words over the cup, with the command to do this in remembrance of him.

passages.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes.
passages.note: Paul says that eating the bread and drinking the cup proclaims the Lord's death until he comes.

passages.quote: Each one must examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup.
passages.note: Paul tells each person to examine himself before eating and drinking.

passages.quote: Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.
passages.note: Paul says that the many who share the one loaf are one body.

readings.label: The bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ: his words at the table say what they are
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Jesus' words “This is My body” and “This is My blood of the covenant” (Matthew 26:26-28) to say what the bread and the cup are once they are set apart for the Supper. They take John 6, where he says his flesh is real food and his blood real drink, together with Paul's “participation in the blood of Christ” and “participation in the body of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:16) and his warning about “sinning against the body and blood of the Lord” (11:27), to speak of the same gift. Catholic teaching, in the Council of Trent (Session 13, chapter 4) and the Catechism (1374-1376), holds that the whole substance of the bread is changed into Christ's body and the whole substance of the wine into his blood, so that the appearances of bread and wine remain, and it calls this change transubstantiation; the Catechism adds that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (1367). Eastern Orthodox churches also confess that the bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Christ. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) and the Longer Catechism of Philaret use the word “transubstantiated”, and each says the word is not to be taken to define the manner of the change (Dositheus, Decree 17; Longer Catechism, questions 339-340); the Orthodox Church in America's teaching on the Eucharist does not use the word and says the mystery defies analysis in rational and logical terms. The Catholic and Orthodox documents therefore agree that the gifts are the body and blood of Christ, and differ in how far the change is explained in terms of substance and appearance.

passages.quote: Take and eat; this is My body.
passages.note: Jesus gives the bread to the disciples and says this is his body; read by holders of this reading as stating what the bread is.

passages.quote: This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
passages.note: Jesus gives the cup and says this is his blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins.
passages.context_note: The next verse names what is in the cup: 'I tell you, I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father's kingdom.' (26:29). The fourth reading quotes it.

passages.quote: Take it; this is My body.
passages.note: Mark's account of the bread, in the same words.

passages.quote: This is My body, given for you
passages.note: Luke's account adds that the body is given for the disciples; the same verse goes on to the command to do this in remembrance of him.

passages.quote: This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.
passages.note: Jesus says the cup is the new covenant in his blood, poured out for the disciples.

passages.quote: This is My body, which is for you
passages.note: Paul passes on the same words over the bread.

passages.quote: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.
passages.note: Jesus says the bread he will give is his flesh, given for the life of the world.

passages.quote: unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you.
passages.note: Jesus says that without eating his flesh and drinking his blood there is no life in a person.
passages.context_note: After the discourse 'many of His disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?”' (6:60), and Jesus says: 'The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life.' (6:63).

passages.quote: For My flesh is real food, and My blood is real drink.
passages.note: Jesus calls his flesh real food and his blood real drink.

passages.quote: Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him.
passages.note: Jesus says that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood remains in him, and he in that person.

passages.quote: Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?
passages.note: Paul asks whether the cup and the bread are a participation in the blood and body of Christ.

passages.quote: whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord.
passages.note: Paul says that eating or drinking unworthily is sin against the body and blood of the Lord.

passages.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
passages.note: Paul says that eating and drinking without recognizing the body brings judgment.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take “is” in Jesus' words to state what the bread and the cup are and not what they stand for: Trent condemns the teaching that Christ is in the sacrament as a sign, a figure or by his power alone (canon 1), and the Confession of Dositheus says the change is real and not figurative. They take the discourse of John 6:51-58 to speak of the gift received in the Supper (Catechism 1384 and 1391; the Confession of Dositheus cites John 6:51 for the Eucharist), and they take 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 to speak of a guilt that comes from receiving what is the body and blood (Catechism 1385; Longer Catechism, question 341). Catholic teaching takes “do this in remembrance of Me” as a memorial in the sense the Catechism gives the word, an act in which the saving event is made present as well as recalled (1362-1363). The fruit of the vine of Matthew 26:29 is not discussed in the documents cited here.

readings.label: The body and blood of Christ are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Jesus' words “This is My body” literally and take the bread and wine to remain bread and wine: his body and blood are present and given with them, and every communicant receives them by mouth. Lutheran documents state this. The Augsburg Confession (Article X) teaches that the body and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed to those who eat the Supper. The Small Catechism calls the sacrament the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ “under the bread and wine”, and the Large Catechism “in and under” them. The Epitome of the Formula of Concord (VII) teaches a sacramental union through which the bread and wine are truly his body and blood, and the Solid Declaration (VII) speaks of the body and blood as present in, under and with the bread. These documents reject transubstantiation (Smalcald Articles III, VI), the Mass as a sacrifice, and the teaching that the bread and wine are bare signs, tokens or memorials (Epitome VII). They say that those without faith also receive the body and blood, to their judgment (Epitome VII; 1 Corinthians 11:27-29), and that forgiveness is received by faith in the words “given and shed for you” (Small Catechism). They rest the presence on Christ's word and on his rule over all things (Epitome VII, citing Ephesians 1:22; Solid Declaration VII, citing Matthew 28:18).

passages.quote: Take and eat; this is My body.
passages.note: Jesus gives the bread and says this is his body; read by holders of this reading in its literal sense.

passages.quote: Take it; this is My body.
passages.note: Mark's account of the bread, in the same words.

passages.quote: and they all drank from it.
passages.note: Mark records that all the disciples drank from the cup.
passages.context_note: The same verse begins: 'Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them', and Jesus' words over the cup follow in 14:24.

passages.quote: This is My body, given for you
passages.note: Luke adds that the body is given for the disciples.

passages.quote: This is My body, which is for you
passages.note: Paul passes on the same words over the bread.

passages.quote: Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?
passages.note: Paul asks whether the cup and the bread are a participation in the blood and body of Christ.

passages.quote: whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord.
passages.note: Paul says that eating or drinking unworthily is sin against the body and blood of the Lord.

passages.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
passages.note: Paul says that eating and drinking without recognizing the body brings judgment.

passages.quote: Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned
passages.note: Jesus says that whoever believes is not condemned and whoever does not believe is already condemned.

passages.quote: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.
passages.note: Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him.

passages.quote: God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all.
passages.note: Paul says God put everything under Christ's feet and made him head over everything for the church.

passages.quote: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.
passages.note: Jesus says all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him.

passages.quote: in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form.
passages.note: Paul says the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ in bodily form.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take John 6:54 and the eating of Christ's flesh in that discourse to speak of the spiritual eating that is faith in the gospel, which the Solid Declaration says happens apart from the Supper and is necessary for salvation, and not of the Supper itself. They take “This is My body” as a statement of what is given and not as a figure, and they reject the saying that Christ's body is too far off in heaven to be present on the earth, pointing to his word and his power (Solid Declaration VII, citing Matthew 28:18; Epitome VII, citing Ephesians 1:22) and reading Acts 3:21 as saying that heaven receives Christ, not that his body is confined to a place there (Solid Declaration VII). They take 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 to say that the unbelieving communicant receives the body and blood to his judgment. They hold, unlike the first reading, that the bread and wine remain, and, unlike the third, that the body and blood are received by mouth and not by faith alone.

readings.label: Christ is truly present to the believer and received by faith through the Holy Spirit: the bread and wine remain, and are the sign and pledge of what they give
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that the believer truly shares in Christ's body and blood in the Supper, by the Holy Spirit and through faith, and take the bread and wine to remain bread and wine, called his body and blood as signs are named by what they give. The Heidelberg Catechism (questions 78-79) says the bread and wine are not changed into Christ's actual body and blood and are visible signs and pledges of them, while the believer shares in Christ by the Spirit. The Belgic Confession (Article 35) says Christ is in heaven and gives himself to believers through faith, who receive his body and blood by the Spirit and not by the mouth, in a manner beyond understanding. The Westminster Confession (29.5-7) says the elements remain bread and wine in substance and that worthy receivers feed on Christ crucified by faith, spiritually, Christ being present to their faith and not bodily in the elements. John Calvin (Institutes IV.17) speaks of a true and substantial communication of Christ's body and blood by the Spirit. The Anglican documents cited here say this in other words (Anglicans differ on the Supper, and the page reads these two): the Thirty-Nine Articles (XXVIII) call the bread “a partaking of the Body of Christ” and say the body is received and eaten “after an heavenly and spiritual manner”, its means faith, and the Anglican Church in North America's catechism (question 133) says the body and blood are truly taken and received in the Lord's Supper by faith. Article XVIII of the Methodist Articles of Religion, held by the United Methodist Church, uses almost the same words. The 1689 London Confession, held by some Baptist bodies, says worthy receivers spiritually receive and feed on Christ crucified, “really and indeed, yet not carnally” (30.7). These documents say that those without faith eat the sign and not Christ (Articles XXIX; Belgic 35; Westminster 29.8).

passages.quote: Take and eat; this is My body.
passages.note: Jesus gives the bread and says this is his body; read by holders of this reading as the way a sign is named by what it gives.

passages.quote: Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?
passages.note: Paul asks whether the cup and the bread are a participation in the blood and body of Christ.

passages.quote: They all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.
passages.note: Paul says Israel in the wilderness ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink, and calls the rock Christ.

passages.quote: The blood on the houses where you are staying will be a sign; when I see the blood, I will pass over you.
passages.note: The Lord names the blood on the houses a sign at the first Passover.

passages.quote: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.
passages.note: Jesus calls himself the bread of life and says whoever comes to and believes in him will not hunger or thirst.

passages.quote: I am the living bread that came down from heaven.
passages.note: Jesus calls himself the living bread that came down from heaven.

passages.quote: Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him.
passages.note: Jesus says that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood remains in him, and he in that person.

passages.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
passages.note: Paul says that eating and drinking without recognizing the body brings judgment.

passages.quote: This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.
passages.note: Two men in white tell the disciples that Jesus was taken into heaven and will come back in the same way.

passages.quote: since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.
passages.note: Paul says Christ is seated at the right hand of God and tells believers to strive for the things above.

passages.quote: our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ
passages.note: Paul says believers await the Lord Jesus Christ as a Savior from heaven.

passages.quote: Heaven must take Him in until the time comes for the restoration of all things
passages.note: Peter says heaven must take Jesus in until the restoration of all things.

passages.quote: Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many
passages.note: The writer says Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many.

passages.quote: we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
passages.note: The writer says believers are sanctified through the sacrifice of Jesus' body once for all.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take “This is My body” as the language in which Scripture names a sign by what it gives, as it names baptism's water a washing of new birth and the Passover blood a sign (Heidelberg Catechism 78, citing Genesis 17:10-11, Exodus 12 and 1 Corinthians 10:1-4; Calvin IV.17.21). They take John 6:51-58 to describe feeding on Christ by faith, which the Supper signs and pledges (Heidelberg Catechism 76 and 79; Calvin IV.17.5, who calls the eating the effect and fruit of faith). They take texts that set Christ in heaven at God's right hand (Acts 1:11; Colossians 3:1; Philippians 3:20) to show where his body is, so that he is received by the Spirit and not in the bread (Heidelberg Catechism 76 and 80; Westminster 29.7; Calvin IV.17.16-19). They take Hebrews 9:25-28 and 10:10-14 to say that Christ's sacrifice was made once, so that the Supper is a remembrance of it and not a repeating (Heidelberg Catechism 80; 1689 Confession 30.2). They take 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 to speak of those who come unworthily receiving the outward elements and not the thing signified, and being guilty before the Lord for it (Westminster 29.8). They take 1 Corinthians 10:16 as a true sharing in Christ, which they say is made by the Spirit.

readings.label: A memorial: the bread and the cup remember and proclaim Christ's death, and the Supper is an ordinance that Christ commanded
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Jesus' command “do this in remembrance of Me” and Paul's “you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes” to say what the Supper is for: believers remember and proclaim his death, and look ahead to his return, with a bread and a cup that stand for his body and blood. Documents that state this include the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (Article VII), which calls the Supper “a symbolic act of obedience” in which members memorialize the death of the Redeemer and look to his second coming; the Articles of Faith of the General Association of Regular Baptist Churches (XV), which call it “the commemoration of His death until He come”; the Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (6b), which calls it a symbol expressing the believer's sharing the divine nature of Christ, a memorial of his suffering and death and a prophecy of his second coming; and the Foursquare Declaration of Faith (IX), which calls the broken bread and the juice of the vine types of Christ's body and shed blood. The Dordrecht Confession (Article X) and the Schleitheim Confession (Article III) speak of the bread and cup in remembrance of his death and body and blood. The Mennonite Church USA confession (Article 12) calls the bread and cup signs and speaks of remembering Jesus' death and God's deliverance, and it also says that the supper re-presents the risen Christ in the church, whose members share in his body and blood, so readers who stand near this reading differ on how Christ's presence is spoken of.

passages.quote: do this in remembrance of Me.
passages.note: Paul passes on Jesus' command, given over the bread, to do this in remembrance of him.

passages.quote: do this in remembrance of Me.
passages.note: Luke records the same command after the words over the bread.

passages.quote: This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.
passages.note: Jesus says the cup is the new covenant in his blood, poured out for the disciples.

passages.quote: I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering.
passages.note: Jesus says he has eagerly desired to eat this Passover with the disciples before he suffers.

passages.quote: Take and eat; this is My body.
passages.note: Jesus gives the bread and says this is his body; read by holders of this reading as the bread standing for his body.

passages.quote: I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father's kingdom.
passages.note: Jesus calls the cup's content the fruit of the vine and speaks of drinking it anew in his Father's kingdom.

passages.quote: I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.
passages.note: The LORD promises a new covenant; read as the covenant Jesus names at the cup.

passages.quote: Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?
passages.note: Paul asks whether the cup and the bread are a participation in the blood and body of Christ.

passages.quote: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too
passages.note: Paul says believers cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.

passages.quote: They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.
passages.note: The first believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer.

passages.quote: On the first day of the week we came together to break bread.
passages.note: Luke records that the disciples at Troas came together on the first day of the week to break bread.

passages.quote: so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature
passages.note: Peter says believers become partakers of the divine nature through God's promises.

passages.quote: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.
passages.note: The angel says those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb are blessed.

readings.answers: The documents of this reading call the bread and the cup symbols or types (the Baptist Faith and Message; the Assemblies of God; the Foursquare Declaration), and holders take Jesus' words “This is My body” and “This is My blood” in that sense. The Dordrecht Confession takes “participation” in 1 Corinthians 10:16 as the unity and fellowship believers have with God and with one another, signified by the breaking of bread, and the Schleitheim Confession echoes 1 Corinthians 10:21 in saying that those who drink the cup of the Lord cannot drink the cup of the devil. The Assemblies of God cites 2 Peter 1:4 for what the symbol expresses, the believer's sharing the divine nature of Christ. They take the words “Do this” as Christ's command and the Supper as an act of obedience to it. They connect the Supper with his return: the Baptist Faith and Message speaks of anticipating his second coming, and the Assemblies of God cites 1 Corinthians 11:26; the documents cited here do not comment on the promise of drinking the fruit of the vine anew (Matthew 26:29). None of the documents cited here comments on John 6, so this page does not state how holders of this reading take it.

terms.term: Lord's Supper, communion, Eucharist, the breaking of bread, the Mass, the Divine Liturgy
terms.note: Names for the same meal. The Lord's Supper is the phrase of 1 Corinthians 11:20, and communion draws on Paul's word “participation” in 10:16. Eucharist, from the Greek word for giving thanks, is the usual word in Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Anglican use. The breaking of bread is the phrase of Acts 2:42. The Mass is the Catholic name for the service at which the Eucharist is celebrated, and the Divine Liturgy the Eastern Orthodox name.

The word for the teaching that the whole substance of the bread and of the wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ while the appearances remain. The Council of Trent and the Catechism of the Catholic Church use it. The Confession of Dositheus and the Longer Catechism of Philaret, both Eastern Orthodox, also use it and say it is not to be taken to define the manner of the change; the Orthodox Church in America's page does not use it. Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Methodist and 1689 Baptist documents reject it.

A phrase for the teaching that Christ himself is present in the Supper. Catholic and Eastern Orthodox documents say the bread and wine become his body and blood, and Lutheran documents say his body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine. Reformed and Anglican documents speak of Christ present to the believer by the Spirit through faith, with the bread and wine remaining. Whether “real” is the right word for that presence is itself a point on which readers differ.

The Lutheran phrase for the way the body and blood of Christ are joined to the bread and wine, so that the bread and wine are truly his body and blood without ceasing to be bread and wine. The phrase “in, with and under” is the common summary of it; the Solid Declaration uses the words “in”, “under” and “with” the bread.

In Reformed, Anglican and Methodist documents, “spiritual” means by the Holy Spirit through faith, and is not meant to say that the presence is less true: the Articles speak of the body received “after an heavenly and spiritual manner”, and the Westminster Confession speaks of Christ present to the faith of believers as really as the elements are to their outward senses (29.7).

The Greek word translated “remembrance” in Luke 22:19 and 1 Corinthians 11:24-25. The Catechism of the Catholic Church says a memorial in Scripture makes a saving event present, while Baptist, Pentecostal and Anabaptist documents speak of a remembrance and commemoration of his death. The readings differ on what the word asks of the one who keeps the Supper.

Three words for the rite. Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist documents call it a sacrament, a rite in which God acts. Eastern Orthodox churches also say holy mystery. Baptist, Pentecostal and Anabaptist documents speak of an ordinance, a rite Christ commanded and his followers obey.

Catholic teaching calls the Eucharist a sacrifice and says the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (Catechism 1367). The Solid Declaration, the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Confession reject the Mass as a sacrifice and say Christ is not offered again. Whether the Supper is a sacrifice is a related point, not one of the readings above.

terms.term: who may receive, and how often
terms.note: Catholic teaching asks those aware of grave sin to receive the sacrament of Reconciliation first and requires communion at least once a year (Catechism 1385, 1389). The Longer Catechism asks each person to examine his conscience and requires communion at least once a year (questions 341, 343). The Large Catechism says the sacrament should be received often. The Mennonite confession invites the baptized who live at peace with God and one another. The Baptist Faith and Message puts baptism before the Supper. These are related points, not readings.
The name often given to the memorial reading, after the Zurich reformer Huldrych Zwingli. The Baptist, Pentecostal and Anabaptist documents cited here do not use it.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 13, Decree on the Most Holy Eucharist, chapters 1-5 and canons 1-6
further_reading.says: It teaches that Christ is truly, really and substantially contained under the appearances of bread and wine (chapter 1), that the whole substance of the bread is changed into his body and of the wine into his blood, which the Church calls transubstantiation (chapter 4, canons 1 and 2), and that he is to be given the worship due to God (chapter 5); canon 1 condemns the teaching that he is present only as a sign, a figure or by his power.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1356-1381 (The Sacramental Sacrifice: Thanksgiving, Memorial, Presence)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 1374 says the whole Christ is truly, really and substantially contained in the Eucharist; paragraph 1376 says the Church calls the change of the whole substance of the bread and wine transubstantiation; paragraphs 1362-1363 say a memorial in Scripture makes a saving event present; and paragraph 1367 says the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1382-1401 (The Paschal Banquet)
further_reading.says: It cites John 6:53 and 6:56-57 and 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 for receiving communion, asks those aware of grave sin to receive the sacrament of Reconciliation first (1385), asks for communion at least once a year (1389), teaches that Christ is whole under either species (1390), and says intercommunion with communities from the Reformation is not possible (1400).

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decree 17
further_reading.says: It teaches that the bread is changed into the true body of the Lord and the wine into his blood, uses the words “transmuted” and “transubstantiated”, adds that the word does not explain the manner of the change, which it calls incomprehensible, and says the change is real and not figurative; it cites Matthew 26:26, 26:28 and John 6:51.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 338-342
further_reading.says: Question 339 says that at the words of institution the bread and wine are changed, or transubstantiated, into the body of Christ; question 340 says the word is not to be taken to define the manner in which they are changed; question 341 asks the communicant to examine his conscience (1 Corinthians 11); question 342 says the communicant is united to Christ and made partaker of everlasting life (John 6:56).

further_reading.title: The Orthodox Faith, Volume II (Worship): The Sacraments, Holy Eucharist (published by the Orthodox Church in America)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the gifts become the real body and blood of Christ, does not use the word transubstantiation, says the mystery defies analysis in rational and logical terms, and rejects the view that the elements are only mental or psychological symbols; it cites John 6 and 1 Corinthians 10 and 11.

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article X (Of the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the body and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord, and it rejects those who teach otherwise.

further_reading.title: Luther's Small Catechism, Part Sixth (The Sacrament of the Altar)
further_reading.says: It answers that the sacrament is the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the bread and wine, instituted by Christ for Christians to eat and drink, and that whoever believes the words “given and shed for you for the remission of sins” has the forgiveness they promise.

further_reading.title: Luther's Large Catechism, Part Fifth (The Sacrament of the Altar)
further_reading.says: It says the sacrament is the true body and blood of Christ in and under the bread and wine, made by the word of Christ joined to the elements, that a sinful minister or communicant still receives the true sacrament while its benefit comes to those who believe the words, and that it should be received often.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Article VII (The Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the body and blood of Christ are truly and essentially present and are distributed and received with the bread and wine through a sacramental union, received by mouth in a heavenly manner and by unbelievers also to their condemnation (1 Corinthians 11:27-29), and it rejects transubstantiation, the Mass as a sacrifice, and the teaching that the bread and wine are mere symbols, tokens, figures or memorials.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article VII (The Holy Supper)
further_reading.says: It speaks of the body and blood as present in, under and with the bread, takes “This is My body” literally and not as a figure, says believers and unbelievers both receive them by mouth, to blessing or to judgment, says the spiritual eating of John 6:54 is faith in the gospel apart from the Supper, and rejects transubstantiation, the Mass as a sacrifice, and the teaching that the elements are mere signs of an absent body.

further_reading.title: Smalcald Articles, Part III, Article VI (Of the Sacrament of the Altar)
further_reading.says: It says the bread and wine in the Supper are the true body and blood of Christ, which godly and wicked Christians both receive, gives the Supper in both forms, and rejects transubstantiation; it cites 1 Corinthians 10:16 and 11:28.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, questions 75-80 (Lord's Days 28-30)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the bread and wine are not changed into Christ's actual body and blood but are visible signs and pledges of them, called his body and blood in the way of sacramental language (78), that believers share in Christ by the Holy Spirit (76, 79), and cites Matthew 26, John 6, 1 Corinthians 10 and 11; the Christian Reformed Church in 2004 and 2006 set aside the last paragraphs of question 80, on the Mass, as no longer binding.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 29 (Of the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: Section 5 says the elements remain bread and wine in substance, section 6 rejects transubstantiation, section 7 says worthy receivers feed on Christ crucified by faith, spiritually, Christ being present to their faith and not bodily in the elements, section 8 says the ignorant and wicked receive only the elements, and section 2 rejects the Mass as a sacrifice.

further_reading.title: Belgic Confession, Article 35 (The Holy Supper of Our Lord Jesus Christ)
further_reading.says: It says Christ gives bread as the sacrament of his body and wine as the sacrament of his blood, that he is in heaven and gives himself to believers through faith, who receive his body and blood by the Spirit and not by the mouth, in a manner beyond understanding, and that the wicked receive the sacrament to their condemnation and not its truth.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 4, chapter 17 (Of the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: Calvin holds that Christ's flesh is life-giving food received by faith through the Spirit (sections 5, 9), argues against transubstantiation (13-15) and against Christ's body being in the bread or everywhere (16-19), and affirms a true and substantial communication of his body and blood; a founder's work, not a church's statement.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Articles XXVIII (Of the Lord's Supper) and XXIX
further_reading.says: Article XXVIII calls the bread broken “a partaking of the Body of Christ” for those who receive rightly and with faith, says transubstantiation “cannot be proved by holy Writ”, and says the Body of Christ is given, taken and eaten “after an heavenly and spiritual manner”, the means being faith; Article XXIX says the wicked do not partake of Christ.

further_reading.title: To Be a Christian: An Anglican Catechism (2019), questions 131-135
further_reading.says: Question 131 says Christ instituted Holy Communion for the continual remembrance of his atoning death and to convey its benefits; question 133 says the inward gift signified is the Body and Blood of Christ, which are truly taken and received in the Lord's Supper by faith (John 6:52-56; 1 Corinthians 10:1-4, 16-18).

further_reading.title: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church, Article XVIII (Of the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It calls the Supper a sacrament of our redemption by Christ's death, says that for those who receive rightly and with faith the bread broken is a partaking of the body of Christ, says transubstantiation cannot be proved from Scripture, and says the body of Christ is given, taken and eaten in the Supper after a heavenly and spiritual manner, faith being the means.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 30 (Of the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 2 calls the Supper a memorial of Christ's one offering and rejects the Mass as a sacrifice; paragraphs 5 and 6 say the elements remain bread and wine in substance and reject transubstantiation; paragraph 7 says worthy receivers spiritually receive and feed on Christ crucified by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally, his body and blood being spiritually present to believing faith (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23-26).

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article VII (Baptism and the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It calls the Lord's Supper a symbolic act of obedience in which church members eat the bread and drink the fruit of the vine to memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate his second coming, after baptism; it cites Matthew 26:26-30, Luke 22:19-20, Acts 2:41-42 and 1 Corinthians 10:16, 21 and 11:23-29.

further_reading.body: General Association of Regular Baptist Churches
further_reading.title: Articles of Faith, Article XV (Baptism and the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It calls the Lord's Supper “the commemoration of His death until He come”, to be preceded always by solemn self-examination, and says the biblical order is baptism and then the Supper, for immersed believers; it cites 1 Corinthians 11:23-28.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths, 6 (The Ordinances of the Church), b. Holy Communion
further_reading.says: It calls the Lord's Supper, of the elements bread and the fruit of the vine, the symbol expressing our sharing the divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 1:4), a memorial of his suffering and death and a prophecy of his second coming (1 Corinthians 11:26), enjoined on all believers “till He come”.

further_reading.title: Foursquare Declaration of Faith, article IX (Water Baptism and the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It speaks of the commemoration and observing of the Lord's Supper by the broken bread, “a precious type of the Bread of Life”, and the juice of the vine, “a blessed type” of the shed blood, calls the observance an ordinance, and asks for self-examination beforehand (1 Corinthians 11:26, 28).

further_reading.body: Dutch Mennonite conference at Dordrecht (1632), later adopted by Mennonites in America (1725)
further_reading.title: Dordrecht Confession of Faith (1632), Article X (Of the Holy Supper)
further_reading.says: It says the Lord instituted the breaking of bread, or Supper, with bread and wine, to be observed in remembrance of his suffering and death and as a sign of the unity and fellowship believers have with God and one another and of the redemption he purchased; it cites Matthew 26:26, Acts 2:42 and 1 Corinthians 10:16 and 11:23, and does not describe a presence in the elements.

further_reading.title: Schleitheim Confession (1527), Article III (the Breaking of Bread)
further_reading.says: It says believers break bread in remembrance of the broken body of Christ and drink the cup as a remembrance of his shed blood, and that only those baptized into the one body of Christ may break the one bread, since they cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of the devil.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 12 (The Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It calls the bread and cup signs of Christ's body given for us and of the new covenant in his blood, says the church thankfully remembers Jesus' death and God's deliverance, and also says the supper re-presents the risen Christ in the church, whose members share in his body and blood; it invites the baptized who live at peace with God and with one another.
